text:
**A Successful Failure: The Flight of Apollo 13**

On April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. It was NASA's third attempt at a lunar landing, and by then the public had begun to think of these flights as routine. The television networks gave the launch only modest coverage. Less than a year after Neil Armstrong's first steps, going to the Moon already seemed like something America simply did.

The crew was led by Jim Lovell, a veteran of three earlier flights who had already orbited the Moon on Apollo 8. With him were Fred Haise, who would pilot the lunar module, and Jack Swigert, who was flying the command module. Swigert had joined the crew only days before launch. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles, and flight doctors would not risk him falling ill in space. Mattingly was grounded and bitterly disappointed. He never caught the measles.

The spacecraft came in two parts that the crew had named. The command module, *Odyssey*, was the cone-shaped capsule where the astronauts lived during the journey and which alone would bring them home through the atmosphere. Attached behind it was the service module, a cylinder holding the main engine, the electrical power system, and the oxygen tanks. Nested ahead of them was the lunar module, *Aquarius*, the spidery craft meant to carry Lovell and Haise down to the hills of Fra Mauro.

For two days the flight went almost perfectly. On the evening of April 13, nearly 56 hours after launch and about 200,000 miles from Earth, the crew finished a television broadcast showing viewers around their cabin. None of the major networks carried it live. A few minutes later, Mission Control in Houston asked Swigert to perform a routine chore: switch on the fans that stirred the supercooled oxygen in the service module's tanks, so the gauges would read accurately.

Swigert flipped the switch. Seconds later the crew heard a loud bang, and the spacecraft shuddered. Warning lights came on. "Okay, Houston," Swigert radioed, "we've had a problem here." Lovell repeated it a moment later: "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first nobody, in space or on the ground, understood how serious it was. Readings on the controllers' screens made so little sense that some suspected faulty instruments. Then Lovell looked out a window and saw a cloud of gas spraying from the side of the spacecraft. "We are venting something out into the space," he reported. The gauges were correct after all. One oxygen tank read empty, and the second was leaking fast.

That oxygen did more than supply air. It fed the three fuel cells that generated *Odyssey*'s electricity and drinking water. Two of the fuel cells were already dead, and the third was failing. Within the hour it was clear that the command module would soon lose all its power. The Moon landing was off, and the only question left was whether the crew could get home alive.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and his team had to work fast. *Odyssey*'s small reentry batteries had to be saved for the end of the flight, because the capsule was the only part of the spacecraft with a heat shield. The crew would have to shut it down completely and move into *Aquarius*. The lunar module would serve as a lifeboat.

It was a lifeboat built for a much shorter trip. *Aquarius* was designed to keep two men alive for about two days on the Moon. Now it had to keep three men alive for about four days, the time it would take to swing around the Moon and fall back to Earth. Every resource had to be stretched: electricity, water, oxygen, and the means of removing the carbon dioxide the astronauts exhaled.

Reaching home was the first problem. Apollo 13 had left the trajectory that would have looped it back to Earth automatically. Nobody trusted the service module's main engine after the explosion, so the crew used the lunar module's descent engine, which had been built to land on the Moon, to put them back on course. Early on April 15 the spacecraft passed behind the Moon, briefly out of radio contact. At their farthest, the three men were about 248,000 miles from home, which is still the farthest any humans have travelled from Earth. Two hours after rounding the Moon, the crew fired the descent engine again to speed up the return and bring them down in the Pacific Ocean, where recovery ships were waiting.

The air itself soon became a threat. The lunar module's canisters of lithium hydroxide, the chemical that absorbed carbon dioxide, could not handle three men for that long. *Odyssey* carried plenty of spare canisters, but they were square, and the openings in *Aquarius* were round. As carbon dioxide levels climbed toward a dangerous point, engineers on the ground worked out a fix using only items they knew were on board: plastic bags, cardboard from the flight manuals, hoses from the spacesuits, and plenty of duct tape. They read the instructions up step by step, and the crew built the improvised adapter, which came to be called the "mailbox." The carbon dioxide readings began to fall.

Life on board was miserable. To save power, almost everything was switched off, including the heaters. Cabin temperatures dropped to around 38 degrees Fahrenheit, and condensation formed on the walls and windows. The men could hardly sleep. Water was rationed so strictly that they became dehydrated, and Haise developed a kidney infection with chills and fever. Even steering was improvised. With the navigation computer powered down, Lovell kept the spacecraft aligned for one course-correction burn by holding the edge of Earth's shadow steady in his window, a technique from an older era of spaceflight.

Meanwhile, the final and most delicate problem waited at the end of the trip. *Odyssey* had been cold and dark for days, and no one had ever planned to restart a command module in flight with so little power. Engineers and astronauts in Houston, Ken Mattingly among them, spent long hours in simulators writing a new power-up sequence that would bring the capsule back to life without draining its batteries. The procedure ran to many pages, and Swigert copied it down by hand.

On April 17, as Earth grew larger in the windows, the crew released the damaged service module. As it drifted away they saw the damage for the first time: an entire side panel had been blown off. "There's one whole side of that spacecraft missing," Lovell reported. Then Swigert brought *Odyssey* back to life, and it worked. The three men climbed into the capsule and released *Aquarius*. "Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you," said a voice from Mission Control.

During reentry, the superheated air around a returning capsule cuts off radio contact for several minutes. This time the blackout lasted longer than expected, and Mission Control fell silent as the seconds ticked by. Then Swigert's voice came through. Minutes later, three orange-and-white parachutes opened over the South Pacific. *Odyssey* splashed down near Samoa, and the crew was lifted aboard the recovery ship USS *Iwo Jima*. Across the world, people who had ignored the launch a week earlier now cheered.

The investigation that followed traced the accident to a chain of small mistakes made years earlier. During ground testing before launch, technicians had left the heaters inside oxygen tank 2 switched on for hours. A thermostat that should have shut them off had never been upgraded to handle the launch pad's higher voltage, so it failed. Temperatures inside the tank rose far beyond normal and damaged the insulation on its wiring. When Swigert switched on the fans in space, the bare wires sparked, and the tank exploded.

NASA redesigned the tanks, and Apollo 14 landed at Fra Mauro the following year. Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, but it is remembered as a "successful failure." It showed that disciplined teamwork and calm ingenuity under pressure could bring three men home from a quarter of a million miles away.
